summary: Jeremy Silva and Chris Hernandez frame their talk around the 'build-operate divide': the gap between product vision and operational reality that causes good AI concepts to fail. They contrast traditional ML with Gen AI, noting decreased barriers to entry, shorter cycle times, and faster iteration speeds, which accentuate the need for a strong ops function. Working across enterprise teams at Freeplay, Jeremy observes companies build prototypes and ship V1s but hit a 'quality chasm' when pushing toward a reliable V2. The only way across is iteration—moving through monitoring, experimentation, testing, and evaluation loops—so product quality becomes a direct function of iteration speed. Chris emphasizes that LLMs hallucinate confidently (joking that one claimed Abraham Lincoln invented Wi-Fi) and fall short on nuance, empathy, and context. Without human-in-the-loop, organizations scale risk rather than productivity. Every human flag or correction is a feedback signal for model refinement. The challenge is that most teams lack enough people to review thousands of outputs. Chris's solution: leverage existing QA and CX teams in contact centers who already evaluate interactions at scale, spot edge cases, and define what good looks like. Their roles evolve from auditors and scorekeepers to model shapers, prompt testers, and AI performance monitors. Gen AI also opens contribution pathways for non-technical domain experts. Jeremy describes an emerging, often unnamed 'AI quality lead' role at successful Gen AI companies, filled by people with deep domain understanding and systems-thinking skills who label data, write evaluation criteria, run experiments, and do prompt engineering—often without writing production code. Even a single empowered individual can make this role meaningful. Chris closes with practical principles: insert HITL at high-risk, high-trust decision points rather than for show; bring ops and CX teams into the lifecycle early to define quality, build golden sets, and test against real-world edge cases; treat launch as the beginning, not the finish line, by tracking performance, flagging hallucination, measuring impact, and iterating; and recognize that scale is about people, not just tech. The overarching takeaway: scaling Gen AI is an operational reliability and responsibility challenge—embedding quality and human feedback with the right people means building faster and better.

takeaways: Gen AI's lower barrier to entry and faster iteration cycles increase, not decrease, the need for a robust AI ops function.

LLMs hallucinate confidently and lack real-world nuance, empathy, and context; without human-in-the-loop, organizations scale risk instead of productivity.
Every human flag or correction is a valuable feedback signal for refining models; HITL should be viewed as a feedback engine, not just a safeguard.
Existing QA and CX/contact-center teams are ideal candidates for evolving into AI model shapers and prompt testers, as they already evaluate interactions at scale and define quality.

An emerging 'AI quality lead' role—combining deep domain knowledge, systems thinking, labeling, evaluation design, and prompt engineering—is becoming critical, even in small teams with just one or two empowered individuals.
HITL should be inserted at high-risk, high-trust decision points rather than for show, especially when resources are limited.
Launch is not the finish line; teams must track performance, flag hallucination, measure impact, and iterate after deployment.
Scaling Gen AI is an operational responsibility, not just a technical challenge; success depends on leveraging QA, ops, support, and frontline teams as strategic partners.

sections.title: Introduction and the Build-Operate Divide
sections.summary: Jeremy and Chris introduce themselves and the talk's premise: good AI product concepts fail due to operational challenges. They aim to show how to bridge product concept and operational reality through evals, human review, and team structure. Jeremy leads product at Freeplay; Chris leads speech analytics at Chime with ~10 years in CX and ~9 in ML.

sections.title: Traditional ML to Gen AI: Lower Barriers, Faster Iteration
sections.summary: Jeremy explains that Gen AI lowers the barrier to entry—less data and shorter training cycles—while increasing iteration speed. This heightened iteration speed accentuates the need for a high-quality ops function. Companies build prototypes, ship V1s, but hit a 'quality chasm' moving to V2. Crossing it requires an iteration loop of monitoring, experimentation, and testing/evaluation; product quality becomes a function of iteration speed. AI ops sits at the foundation, requiring significant human elbow grease.

sections.title: Human-in-the-Loop and Hallucination Risk
sections.summary: Chris shares an anecdote where an LLM claimed Abraham Lincoln invented Wi-Fi, illustrating confident hallucination. He argues LLMs fall short on nuance, empathy, and context without humans. Without HITL, you scale risk not productivity. Every human flag or correction is a feedback signal for model refinement; HITL should be viewed as a feedback engine, not just a safeguard. A key challenge: most teams lack enough people to review thousands of outputs.

sections.title: QA and CX Teams as Model Shapers
sections.summary: Chris proposes leveraging existing QA and CX/contact-center teams who already evaluate interactions at scale, spot edge cases, and define quality. Their roles are evolving from retrospective auditing and scorekeeping to shaping model behavior, testing prompts, and monitoring AI performance. Gen AI opens doors for non-technical domain experts—like a wine connoisseur who need not be a winemaker. A diagram shows QA scope expanding from core auditing into prompt testing and output tagging.

sections.title: The Emerging AI Quality Lead Role
sections.summary: Jeremy describes an emerging, often unnamed 'AI quality lead' role seen at successful Gen AI companies, exemplified by Chris's team. People in this role come from product, ops, or engineering backgrounds and share deep domain understanding and systems-thinking skills. Day-to-day they label data, write evaluation criteria, run experiments, and do prompt engineering—often without writing production code. This role can exist with one or two people in smaller organizations and scale up in enterprises.

sections.title: Closing Principles and Key Takeaways
sections.summary: Chris closes with practical principles for scaling Gen AI. Even a single or couple empowered individuals can form a meaningful quality team. HITL should be inserted at high-risk, high-trust decision points, not just for show. Ops and CX teams should be brought into the lifecycle early to define quality, build golden sets, and test against real-world edge cases. Launch is not the finish line but the beginning—teams must track performance, flag hallucination, measure impact, and iterate. Scale is about people, not just tech; QA, ops, support, and frontline teams should be strategic partners. The overarching takeaway: scaling Gen AI is an operational reliability and responsibility, and embedding quality and human feedback with the right people means building faster and better.

demonstrations: Chris's anecdote of typing 'who invented Wi-Fi?' into an early LLM and receiving 'Abraham Lincoln,' illustrating confident hallucination.
Diagram shown depicting how QA scope is expanding from core auditing into Gen AI prompt testing, output tagging, and model behavior shaping.
limitations: Most teams don't have enough people to review thousands of model outputs, making it hard to improve and even measure current model state.
Model-graded evaluations are useful but still require the human element, which is resource-constrained.
Limited HITL resources mean organizations should prioritize inserting human review at high-risk, high-trust decision points rather than attempting blanket coverage.
quantitativeClaims: Chris has approximately 10 years in CX and about 9 years in ML.
QA professionals were listening to phone calls and evaluating interactions 25 years ago, representing the historical baseline for the role.
